conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to help you feel supported and to check in on how you’re doing emotionally now that your baby has arrived.  

To do that, I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything we discuss stays confidential, and you can take your time.  

I’ll read each question aloud in everyday language; just tell me how you’ve been feeling. Ready to start?

**1.** Over the last week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, not very often. I used to laugh a lot before the baby—now, even when my partner tries to be funny, I’ll smile a bit, but it feels forced. I chuckled once when the baby made a silly face, but it was brief. Most of the time I’m too tired or preoccupied to find things genuinely funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really. I’ll give a little smile if something’s obviously funny, but it’s like the laugh gets stuck—nothing feels truly amusing anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Sometimes. I’ll catch myself looking forward to small stuff—like my mom bringing dinner or a quiet moment with coffee—but most days it feels more like “I guess that’ll be nice” than real excitement.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. When the baby wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or holding him the way he needs. It’s silly, but the thought pops in even when I know babies just cry.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. I’ll be sitting there with the baby sleeping soundly, but my mind races—what if he stops breathing, what if I’m missing some sign that he’s sick? It’s like there’s always a low hum of worry even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times. Once, right after I put him down in the crib, my heart just started racing and I felt shaky, like something awful was about to happen even though the room was quiet and he was fine. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me unsettled.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the week. Between feedings, laundry, and trying to grab sleep in tiny bits, it feels like the day’s chores pile up faster than I can clear them. Some mornings I look at the mess and just want to crawl back under the blanket, though I still push through.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights. I’m exhausted, but when the house is finally quiet my mind keeps circling—worrying about the baby, replaying everything I did that day, wondering if I’m cut out for this. It takes me a long time to drift off, and then he wakes up twenty minutes later.
I have felt sad or miserable

Off and on—maybe every other day. It’s not constant, but I’ll suddenly feel this heavy sadness, like I’m missing something or I’m not doing motherhood the way I should. It usually lifts when the baby smiles or when my partner hugs me, but it keeps creeping back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Only once this week. It was the night he cluster-fed for hours and I couldn’t get him to sleep—I sat on the couch, tears just rolled down, mostly from sheer tiredness and frustration. Most days I hold it in, but that night the dam broke for a minute.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself—I just want to feel like me again.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Anhedonia (Q1, Q2) – minimal capacity for genuine amusement or excitement  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame (Q3) – attributes infant crying to maternal failure  
- Persistent generalized anxiety & situational panic symptoms without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / difficulty coping with daily tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent insomnia – trouble falling/staying asleep related to rumination and worry (Q7)  
- Intermittent sadness or tearfulness, occurring several times/week (Q8, Q9)

Patterns:
Low mood, loss of pleasure, heightened anxiety, and functional overload consistent with possible postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features.

Risk indicators:
- Sleep disturbance directly linked to mood/anxiety  
- Frequent worry and situational panic  
- Episodic crying and self-doubt; no current self-harm ideation (Q10 denied)

Safety:
Patient explicitly denies thoughts of self-harm; no suicidal content elicited.

Summary:
Screening reveals multiple symptoms meeting threshold for further evaluation of perinatal mood/anxiety disorder; no immediate safety concerns identified. Recommend formal assessment with standardized tool (e.g., EPDS) and referral for appropriate perinatal mental health follow-up.
